latin: Nomen dei quatuor litterarum, quod est ex mem, sade, pe, et sa/de, regno Dauidis debet appropriari.
translation: The four-letter name of God, made up of mem, tsade, pe, and tsade, ought to be appropriated to the kingdom of David.
translation_note: This 'name of four letters' is not the Tetragrammaton YHVH itself but a different combination (mem-tsade-pe-tsade), generated, per Farmer's note, by replacing each letter of YHVH with its counterpart under a reversed Hebrew alphabet — Pico's so-called revolutio alphabetariae (paraphrase; farmer1998:18155). 'regno Dauidis' ('kingdom of David') is identified by Farmer as the tenth sefirah (paraphrase; farmer1998:18155).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-swarm-batch3, from Latin at farmer1998:18082

sources.pico_relation: identified by Wirszubski as the direct source of thesis 28.29 ('Conclusio xxix'), as against theses whose Bahir content may only be mediated through Recanati

doctrine: Thesis 28.29 assigns the four-letter divine name formed from mem, tsade, pe, and tsade to 'the kingdom of David' (farmer1998:18082). Farmer's note identifies 'kingdom of David' with 'the tenth sefirah', and explains the four-letter name as generated by substituting each letter of the ineffable name YHVH (normally the sixth sefirah) with its counterpart under a reversed Hebrew alphabet, citing 'Anagnine (1937: 160), Wirszubski (1989: 43-44)' (paraphrase; farmer1998:18155).
context: Farmer's cross-reference apparatus ties the thesis to the immediately preceding 28.28, on the 'volatile' creature of the fifth day understood as worldly angels visible to men (farmer1998:18078).
reception: Wirszubski quotes the thesis in full as his 'Conclusio XXIX' (wirszubski1989:2460, 2463, 7256) and situates it within a source-critical argument about the Bahir and Recanati.
historiography: Wirszubski uses the thesis as a test case for distinguishing Pico's direct and indirect sources: "Conclusio xxix, which was inspired by the Bahir, is a case in point. It treats of the proper application of the name MSPS and is located between two theses both of which treat of angels" (wirszubski1989:3177). He generalizes: "It is certain that Pico read the Bahir: Scholem proved it beyond doubt" (wirszubski1989:3284), while noting that of the theses reflecting the Bahir, 'only one (Conclusio xxix) derives in all likelihood from the Bahir itself', the others being possibly mediated through Recanati's commentary (paraphrase; wirszubski1989:3284).

quotations.text: Conclusio xxix, which was inspired by the Bahir, is a case in point. It treats of the proper application of the name MSPS and is located between two theses both of which treat of angels.
It is certain that Pico read the Bahir: Scholem proved it beyond doubt.

not_established: The exact transliteration of the four-letter combination is uncertain: theses.json/Farmer's OCR gives 'sa/de' for the repeated letter, and Wirszubski's own excerpt renders the name with an evident OCR corruption ('fSXo MS PS'); which reading is correct is not established from the sources consulted beyond Farmer's gloss 'mem tzade pe tzade' (paraphrase; farmer1998:18155).
The Anagnine (1937) reference cited by Farmer was not itself consulted; only Farmer's citation of it is recorded here (paraphrase; farmer1998:18155).
